context: A box contains coloured blocks of four colours: purple, orange, white and pink. One block is selected at random.
stem: A box contains coloured blocks: ${=pu}$ purple, ${=og}$ orange, ${=wh}$ white and ${=pn}$ pink. A block is selected at random. What is the probability that the block is neither purple nor white? Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
solution: Count all the blocks in the box: ${=pu}+{=og}+{=wh}+{=pn}={=n}$ blocks.

A block that is neither purple nor white is the complement of a block that is purple or white. The number of purple or white blocks is ${=pu}+{=wh}={=pu + wh}$, so $P(\text{purple or white})=\frac{{=pu + wh}}{{=n}}$.
An event and its complement have probabilities that add up to $1$, so $P(\text{neither purple nor white})=1-P(\text{purple or white})=1-\frac{{=pu + wh}}{{=n}}=\frac{{=n - (pu + wh)}}{{=n}}$.
Check: the orange and pink blocks number ${=og}+{=pn}={=og + pn}$, which agrees. In simplest form, $P(\text{neither purple nor white})=\frac{{=numerator(f)}}{{=denominator(f)}}$.
notes: Advanced twist taken from the book's ex14-8-17f (neither orange nor pink, answered as 1 minus the probability of 'orange or pink'), here with four colour counts so the student must total the blocks, add two colours and take the complement. The colours are fixed (purple/orange/white/pink, the box of blocks in ex14-8-11d); only the four counts vary (8 to 40 each, total at most 160). The answer is a proper fraction, asked in simplest form, so it is unambiguous and avoids the intermediate-rounding trap of the book's decimal answers. Step 4 always states the reduced fraction even when the fraction is already in lowest terms. No misconceptions are catalogued for this objective, so none are attached; the family has no distractors.
